newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's King Hussein turns to old guard peacemaker.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's King Hussein turns to old guard peacemaker.

text.p: King Hussein has picked veteran former premier Abdul-Salam al-Majali, who brokered Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, to replace outgoing reformist Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.

Officials said the appointment of 71-year-old Majali, who has good relations with the Jewish state, suggested Kabariti had been dismissed after a crisis with Israel, brought to a head by a soldier's killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls last week.
"Majali sends a strong message that the kingdom puts uppermost priority to its special strategic ties with the Jewish state," a political analyst said.
Kabariti was appointed in February last year with a mandate for sweeping economic and administrative reform.

Officials said Majali, a tribal leader from the southern citadel town of Karak, was the only candidate with the experience to lead what is widely expected to be a caretaker government focussing on closer ties with Israel.
"The king is returning to the old guard," one official said.

Majali, who hails from a powerful East Bank Karak tribe with strong ties to the king, led Jordan's peace talks team with Israel before becoming prime minister in 1993. One year later he put his signature on a peace treaty ending Jordan's official 46-year state of war with Israel.

Majali will put further emphasis on Jordan's commitment to the peace treaty which has been shaken by Kabariti's strong criticism of Israel's settlement policy in Jerusalem and accusations of footdragging on peace accords with Palestinians.
With strong backing from the king, Kabariti's government last August weathered its worst domestic crisis after civil disturbances broke out in the south when bread prices were raised.

But 47-year-old Kabariti, a new breed of prime minister who broke the mould of traditional Jordanian politics, appears to have finally fallen out with King Hussein over handling Israeli ties as Middle East tension grew, officials said.

They said Kabariti angered King Hussein by adopting a harder line on Israel than the king would have liked. This along with fears that Kabariti's increasing rapprochement with the Palestinians may jeopardise ties with Israel, appear to have motivated his dismissal, they said.

Matters came to a head after Thursday's shooting of Israeli schoolgirls by a lone Jordanian soldier, which enraged King Hussein, who was moved to act vigorously to contain its repercussions on strategic ties.
"Kabariti's views over how to handle ties with Israel ran counter to His Majesty's and their differences became unbridgeable after the (soldier) shooting," one official told Reuters.
Majali's return could signal a cooler relationship with the Palestinians than with Kabariti, who helped mend ties with PLO leader Yasser Arafat after years of mistrust, officials said.
Majali also oversaw in 1993 Jordan's first multi-party elections for decades -- a role he is likely to repeat in the next elections scheduled for November.

Majali's government will have to walk a number of domestic tightropes, including containing the powerful Islamist opposition whom many fear will capitalise on widespread disappointment by Jordanians over the few gains from peace with Israel.
